subject: the 8 percent vacancy rule
preheader: fully occupied is a fantasy. here's what to actually budget.
headline: Vacancy isn't pessimism. It's accounting.
body: Every property is vacant sometimes. Tenant moves out, two weeks to clean and turn, a month to lease. Even a stable rental in a great market loses 3-5% to vacancy and turnover. Most properties lose closer to 8%.

Markets differ. Class A suburbs in Nashville or Raleigh might genuinely run 4-5% vacancy. Class C properties in soft Midwest markets routinely hit 10-12%. Short-term rentals can hit 30%+ in shoulder months.

Why this matters: take a $1,800/mo rental, $21,600 gross. At 5% vacancy you lose $1,080/yr. At 10% you lose $2,160/yr. That $1,080 difference is the entire margin between a 'good' and 'mediocre' deal once you net out expenses. People who underwrite at 0% vacancy are lying to themselves by exactly one nice vacation a year.
My default: I model 8% vacancy unless I have a reason to go lower. If the seller says 'never been vacant', I add 8% anyway. If the market is genuinely tight, I'll go to 5%. Rarely below.
TrueCap defaults vacancy to a market-specific value when you paste an address. You can override it, but the default is honest.
